title: View System Internals (V1)
scopeHtml: Measure/layout/draw, MeasureSpec, invalidation, custom views and ViewGroups, touch dispatch, nested scrolling, layout optimisation, overdraw, view binding, hardware layers.

questions.promptHtml: What is a MeasureSpec, what are its three modes, and how do match_parent, wrap_content and a fixed dp map onto them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the entry test for custom-view competence. People who have never written onMeasure cannot answer it precisely.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A MeasureSpec is one 32-bit int a parent hands a child. The top 2 bits are the mode and the low 30 bits are a size. EXACTLY means "be this size", AT_MOST means "any size up to this", UNSPECIFIED means "no limit, tell me what you want". A fixed dp becomes EXACTLY, match_parent becomes EXACTLY with the parent's size (or AT_MOST if the parent itself is AT_MOST), and wrap_content becomes AT_MOST with the parent's available size.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The parent builds the child's spec in ViewGroup.getChildMeasureSpec(parentSpec, padding, childDimension) from two inputs: its own spec and the child's LayoutParams.

child LayoutParams ->   parent EXACTLY(100)   parent AT_MOST(100)   parent UNSPECIFIED
fixed 40px             EXACTLY(40)            EXACTLY(40)           EXACTLY(40)
match_parent           EXACTLY(100)           AT_MOST(100)          UNSPECIFIED(0)*
wrap_content           AT_MOST(100)           AT_MOST(100)          UNSPECIFIED(0)*
(* size depends on API level and the sUseZeroUnspecifiedMeasureSpec flag for old targets)

Padding is subtracted from the parent size first. The child then picks a measured size and must call setMeasuredDimension(). The parent is free to ignore it in layout(), but well-behaved ViewGroups do not. Because the mode lives in the high bits you decode with MeasureSpec.getMode()/getSize(), never with arithmetic. UNSPECIFIED appears under ScrollView/HorizontalScrollView children and in RecyclerView wrap_content measurement.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onMeasure(wSpec: Int, hSpec: Int) {
    val desiredW = suggestedMinimumWidth + paddingLeft + paddingRight + textWidthPx.toInt()
    val desiredH = suggestedMinimumHeight + paddingTop + paddingBottom + textHeightPx.toInt()
    // resolveSize handles EXACTLY / AT_MOST / UNSPECIFIED correctly
    setMeasuredDimension(resolveSize(desiredW, wSpec), resolveSize(desiredH, hSpec))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring the mode and returning MeasureSpec.getSize() always: wrap_content then behaves like match_parent (the classic custom-view bug).
  • Forgetting padding in the desired size.
  • Not calling setMeasuredDimension (throws IllegalStateException: View with id ... did not call setMeasuredDimension()).
  • Treating AT_MOST as "must be this size".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does resolveSize do? → EXACTLY: returns spec size. AT_MOST: min(desired, specSize). UNSPECIFIED: desired.
  2. What is resolveSizeAndState? → Same plus MEASURED_STATE_TOO_SMALL flag so a parent can re-measure.
  3. Why can a child be measured with different specs in one pass? → Parents such as LinearLayout with weight and RelativeLayout measure twice; see the layout-passes question.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites the three modes. Senior explains the parent-derived mapping table, that the spec is parent-negotiated rather than a child request, and the UNSPECIFIED cases.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom chart view that always returned its spec size filled the whole screen inside a wrap_content card on tablets, and was only noticed on large devices.

questions.promptHtml: Explain invalidate(), requestLayout() and postInvalidate(). When do you call each in a custom view?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Wrong choice wastes frames (needless measure) or leaves stale pixels (missing draw).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: invalidate() marks a region dirty so the view is redrawn on the next frame, with no measure/layout. requestLayout() marks the view and its ancestors for a new measure and layout pass, which then also redraws if bounds change. postInvalidate() is invalidate() that is safe from a non-UI thread. I call invalidate() when only appearance changed, requestLayout() when the size or position of the view may change, and postInvalidate() from a background thread.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• invalidate() must run on the UI thread. It sets PFLAG_DIRTY, propagates the dirty rect up through invalidateChild/invalidateChildInParent to ViewRootImpl, which schedules a traversal on the next VSYNC via Choreographer. With hardware acceleration only invalidated views re-record their display list.
  • requestLayout() sets PFLAG_FORCE_LAYOUT on the view and walks to the root setting the flag on each ancestor, then ViewRootImpl.requestLayout() schedules a traversal. Ancestors' measure caches are cleared, so the whole ancestor chain re-measures (siblings that did not change may reuse cached specs and skip onMeasure).
  • postInvalidate() posts through a handler to the UI thread. It is not a frame scheduler. Calling it in a tight loop is a busy loop.
  • Many setters (setText, setPadding, setVisibility) already call the right one. TextView.setText calls requestLayout only when the layout size can change.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var progress = 0f
    set(v) { if (field != v) { field = v; invalidate() } }          // draw only

var label = ""
    set(v) { if (field != v) { field = v; requestLayout(); invalidate() } } // size may change

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling requestLayout() for color/progress changes: whole ancestor chain re-measures each frame.
  • Calling invalidate() inside onDraw unconditionally: infinite redraw loop, 100% frame work.
  • Calling invalidate() off the UI thread: CalledFromWrongThreadException (or silent corruption on some paths).
  • Calling requestLayout() inside onLayout/onMeasure of the same view: re-entrancy, Android logs "requestLayout() improperly called".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does requestLayout() always redraw? → Not by itself. If measured size and position end up unchanged, no draw is guaranteed; call invalidate() too if content changed.
  2. invalidate(Rect) use? → Deprecated in API 28+ because hardware rendering ignores dirty regions; view-level invalidation is what matters.
  3. Why does requestLayout cost grow with depth? → Flags propagate to the root and every flagged ancestor re-runs onMeasure/onLayout, so deep trees amplify it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE gives the one-liner rule. Senior adds the propagation mechanics, VSYNC coalescing (many calls per frame collapse into one traversal) and the cost model.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An animated progress ring called requestLayout() per tick; Layout Inspector/Perfetto showed measure taking 4 ms per frame in a list of 20 rings. Switching to invalidate() removed it.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through building a production-quality custom View: constructors, attributes, measuring, drawing and what you must not do in onDraw.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Custom views reveal whether you understand the framework contract rather than just using widgets.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Use @JvmOverloads constructors with (context, attrs, defStyleAttr), read attributes from obtainStyledAttributes and recycle the array (or use use {}), allocate Paint/Path once as fields, implement onMeasure with resolveSize, size-dependent geometry in onSizeChanged, draw in onDraw without allocating, and call invalidate/requestLayout correctly when properties change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Lifecycle order: constructor, onAttachedToWindow, onMeasure (one or more), onSizeChanged, onLayout, onDraw (many), onDetachedFromWindow. Precompute geometry (Path, gradient shaders, text layouts) in onSizeChanged, since onDraw runs every frame and the Android docs explicitly warn against creating Paint/Path in draw methods: it forces GC and bypasses hardware pipeline caches. Hardware-accelerated paths rebuild a texture mask whenever a Path changes, so mutate Paths sparingly.

Attributes: declare <declare-styleable>, pull from attrs and defStyleAttr (so theme styles work). Provide contentDescription and accessibility semantics where meaningful. Handle RTL with layoutDirection. Stop animators in onDetachedFromWindow to avoid leaks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class RingView @JvmOverloads constructor(
    ctx: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? = null, defStyle: Int = R.attr.ringViewStyle
) : View(ctx, attrs, defStyle) {
    private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply { style = Paint.Style.STROKE }
    private val oval = RectF()
    var sweep = 0f
        set(v) { field = v.coerceIn(0f, 360f); invalidate() }

    init {
        ctx.obtainStyledAttributes(attrs, R.styleable.RingView, defStyle, 0).use {
            paint.strokeWidth = it.getDimension(R.styleable.RingView_ringWidth, 8f * resources.displayMetrics.density)
            paint.color = it.getColor(R.styleable.RingView_ringColor, Color.BLUE)
        }
    }
    override fun onSizeChanged(w: Int, h: Int, ow: Int, oh: Int) {
        val inset = paint.strokeWidth / 2
        oval.set(paddingLeft + inset, paddingTop + inset, w - paddingRight - inset, h - paddingBottom - inset)
    }
    override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) { c.drawArc(oval, -90f, sweep, false, paint) }
}

(TypedArray.use requires API 31+ AutoCloseable or the AndroidX/Kotlin use for Closeable; on older APIs call recycle() in try/finally. Verify against your minSdk.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Allocating Paint/RectF/Path in onDraw.
  • Hard-coded pixel sizes instead of dp.
  • Skipping the 3-arg constructor, so styles/themes do not apply.
  • Forgetting to recycle the TypedArray.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why onSizeChanged and not onMeasure for geometry? → Final size is only known there; onMeasure may run several times with provisional specs.
  2. How do you make it animatable with ObjectAnimator? → Provide a property with a setter (sweep) that calls invalidate().
  3. How do you test a custom view? → Robolectric/Paparazzi/Roborazzi screenshot tests plus Espresso for touch; verify tool choice for your project.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE writes it so it draws. Senior covers theming (defStyleAttr), geometry in onSizeChanged, accessibility, RTL, detach cleanup and draw-path allocation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A badge view allocated a Paint per draw in a feed; allocation profiler showed 40 MB/min churn and periodic 15 ms GC pauses during scroll.

questions.promptHtml: Describe the three traversal passes of the View system. Why can measure run more than once, and why is layout_weight a performance concern?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about why a particular XML layout is slow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ViewRootImpl.performTraversals runs measure (each view computes its size from parent specs), layout (parent assigns each child's left/top/right/bottom) and draw (record or execute drawing). Measure may run multiple times because some parents (LinearLayout with weights, RelativeLayout, ConstraintLayout in some cases, FrameLayout with match_parent children) measure children twice, and nested such parents multiply to exponential cost. The official docs say nesting LinearLayouts with weights is especially expensive because each child is measured twice.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Choreographer VSYNC -> ViewRootImpl.doTraversal -> performTraversals
   measure : root.measure(spec) -> onMeasure -> children.measure(...)   (top-down, recursive)
   layout  : root.layout(l,t,r,b) -> onLayout -> children.layout(...)
   draw    : root.draw(canvas)   -> display list recorded, handed to RenderThread

Double taxation: LinearLayout with weightSum or any weighted child measures non-weighted children first, then re-measures weighted ones with leftover space. Two nested levels -> 2x2 = 4 measures of the leaf; depth d -> 2^d. RelativeLayout also does two passes (horizontal then vertical dependency graph). Mitigation: flatten with ConstraintLayout (one solve, mostly linear), avoid weights in deep chains, use Space/guidelines, and use lint's "NestedWeights" check. Lint's default deep-layout threshold is depth 10 per the official layout-optimisation guide.

A view skips re-measure when specs equal the cached spec and no FORCE_LAYOUT flag is set. This is why requestLayout is expensive and why layout stability helps lists.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<!-- Costly: nested weights, leaf measured 4x -->
<LinearLayout android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:weightSum="2">
  <LinearLayout android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_weight="1" android:layout_height="wrap_content" android:weightSum="2">
    <TextView android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_weight="1" android:layout_height="wrap_content"/>
  </LinearLayout>
</LinearLayout>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming measure is O(n) always.
  • Using layout_weight for equal-width columns in every RecyclerView item.
  • Calling getWidth() in onMeasure (zero at that time).
  • Reading measuredWidth after requestLayout but before the next pass.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect double taxation? → Layout Inspector's measure/layout/draw indicators, Perfetto measure/layout slices, lint, or Trace counts per view class.
  2. Is ConstraintLayout always faster? → No: for trivially shallow layouts it can be slower than a FrameLayout; it wins on flat but complex designs. Measure, do not assume.
  3. Does draw re-run if only layout changed? → Views whose bounds changed re-record display lists; unchanged children replay.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE names the three phases. Senior quantifies the multiplicative measure cost and ties it to requestLayout and RecyclerView item inflation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A settings screen built from nested weighted LinearLayouts took 38 ms to first draw on a low-end device; flattening to ConstraintLayout cut measure to 9 ms.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate ships SparkLine, a custom view used in a RecyclerView of 30 visible rows. After release, p95 scroll frame time went from 9 ms to 24 ms on a mid-range device (60 Hz, 16.6 ms budget), and the view is full-screen width even when XML says wrap_content. Code:

class SparkLine(ctx: Context, attrs: AttributeSet?) : View(ctx, attrs) {
    var points: List<Float> = emptyList()
        set(v) { field = v; requestLayout() }

    override fun onMeasure(w: Int, h: Int) {
        setMeasuredDimension(MeasureSpec.getSize(w), MeasureSpec.getSize(h))
    }

    override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) {
        val paint = Paint().apply { color = Color.GREEN; strokeWidth = 3f }
        val path = Path()
        points.forEachIndexed { i, y -> if (i == 0) path.moveTo(0f, y) else path.lineTo(i * 10f, y) }
        canvas.drawPath(path, paint)
        invalidate()
    }
}

Red herring: the adapter uses notifyDataSetChanged() which is wasteful, but the profiler shows the time is in SparkLine.
questions.promptHtml: List every bug, in order of impact, and show the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move Paint out of onDraw." Misses the invalidate() loop and the wrap_content bug, and does not explain why the hot cost is measure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the XML width wrap_content? (explains the full-width bug). How often does points change per row? Does the view animate? What minSdk? (affects TypedArray and hardware path support).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the unconditional invalidate(). That alone stops 30 views redrawing every frame forever.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) invalidate() in onDraw = permanent redraw loop. (b) requestLayout() for a draw-only change = ancestor re-measure per bind. (c) Allocation of Paint/Path per draw = GC churn. (d) onMeasure ignores mode.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto trace: continuous Choreographer#doFrame with draw slices even when idle; Layout Inspector; allocation profiler for Paint/Path; confirm the wrap_content bug by looking at the measured size in Layout Inspector.
  5. Root cause: onDraw calling invalidate() schedules another traversal next VSYNC, so the app never idles. requestLayout cascades up the RecyclerView item and RecyclerView itself. onMeasure returns the spec size regardless of mode, so AT_MOST fills.
  6. Fix: Short-term: delete invalidate() from onDraw, swap requestLayout() for invalidate(). Long-term: fields for paint/path, rebuild path only in the setter, use resolveSize.
  7. Prevention: Lint rule DrawAllocation (on by default), a screenshot test with wrap_content, a Perfetto check for "no frames when idle" in macrobenchmark.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not switch to Compose Canvas just for this; the bug is in the contract, not the toolkit. I would not cache a Bitmap unless profiling shows path building dominates.
class SparkLine @JvmOverloads constructor(ctx: Context, attrs: AttributeSet? = null) : View(ctx, attrs) {
    private val paint = Paint(Paint.ANTI_ALIAS_FLAG).apply { color = Color.GREEN; strokeWidth = 3f; style = Paint.Style.STROKE }
    private val path = Path()
    var points: List<Float> = emptyList()
        set(v) { field = v; rebuildPath(); invalidate() }
    private fun rebuildPath() {
        path.rewind()
        points.forEachIndexed { i, y -> if (i == 0) path.moveTo(0f, y) else path.lineTo(i * 10f, y) }
    }
    override fun onMeasure(w: Int, h: Int) {
        val dw = (points.size * 10) + paddingLeft + paddingRight
        setMeasuredDimension(resolveSize(dw, w), resolveSize(48 * resources.displayMetrics.density.toInt(), h))
    }
    override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) { c.drawPath(path, paint) }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if points changes every frame? → Still invalidate() only; consider drawing into a Picture/RenderNode or limiting redraw rate.
  • Will setLayerType(HARDWARE) help? → Only if the content is static while transformed; here content changes, so it adds texture uploads.
  • Why was the first-fix p95 not fully back to 9 ms? → notifyDataSetChanged still rebinds everything; fix with DiffUtil (see RecyclerView chunk).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sparkline used in a portfolio list kept the device from entering idle; battery stats showed the app at 4% per hour while in the foreground doing nothing. One stray invalidate() in onDraw.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Only moves Paint; keeps invalidate/requestLayout.
  • Hire: Finds the invalidate loop and requestLayout misuse; fixes measure mode.
  • Strong hire: Also explains propagation cost, adds idle-frame check to benchmarks and flags path rebuilding cost.

questions.promptHtml: How does a custom View save and restore its state across configuration change and process death? Why do two instances of the same view sometimes show the same state after restore?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: State bugs after rotation in custom views are common and subtle; this separates people who know the id-keyed SparseArray mechanism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: View hierarchy state is saved via dispatchSaveInstanceState into a SparseArray<Parcelable> keyed by view id. A view participates if it has an id, isSaveEnabled is true, and it overrides onSaveInstanceState/onRestoreInstanceState returning a BaseSavedState subclass. Two views with the same id (or no id) collide or are skipped, which causes cloned or lost state, typically in includes, adapters or ViewPagers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity/Fragment calls window.saveHierarchyState, which calls dispatchSaveInstanceState on the root; each ViewGroup calls it on children. A view with NO_ID is skipped. The state goes into the activity's saved-state bundle (so it is subject to the Binder transaction limit, around 1 MB shared per process, see the process-death chunk in A2). Restore is by id lookup, so duplicated ids (the same layout included twice without distinct ids, or custom views inflated in RecyclerView items) restore the same Parcelable into several views.

Fix duplicates by giving instances unique ids, or (for a composite ViewGroup) by overriding dispatchSaveInstanceState/dispatchRestoreInstanceState to call dispatchFreezeSelfOnly/dispatchThawSelfOnly, which keeps the composite's state private (verify exact behaviour on your minSdk). RecyclerView items are not restored through this path; hold item state in the model/ViewModel.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CounterView(ctx: Context, attrs: AttributeSet?) : View(ctx, attrs) {
    var count = 0
    override fun onSaveInstanceState(): Parcelable =
        SavedState(super.onSaveInstanceState(), count)
    override fun onRestoreInstanceState(state: Parcelable?) {
        if (state is SavedState) { super.onRestoreInstanceState(state.superState); count = state.count }
        else super.onRestoreInstanceState(state)
    }
    class SavedState : BaseSavedState {
        val count: Int
        constructor(superState: Parcelable?, count: Int) : super(superState) { this.count = count }
        private constructor(p: Parcel) : super(p) { count = p.readInt() }
        override fun writeToParcel(out: Parcel, flags: Int) { super.writeToParcel(out, flags); out.writeInt(count) }
        companion object { @JvmField val CREATOR = object : Parcelable.Creator<SavedState> {
            override fun createFromParcel(p: Parcel) = SavedState(p)
            override fun newArray(n: Int) = arrayOfNulls<SavedState>(n) } }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No android:id: nothing is saved.
  • Not calling super in save/restore: the View base state (e.g., focus) is lost.
  • Saving large data (bitmaps, lists) into the view state, risking TransactionTooLargeException.
  • Expecting restore before onAttachedToWindow; restore happens after inflation, around onRestoreInstanceState of the host.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. setSaveEnabled(false) use? → Opt out for transient/derived state or duplicates.
  2. Why does EditText keep text across rotation without code? → TextView has its own SavedState and freezesText; it needs an id.
  3. How does this differ in Compose? → rememberSaveable with a Saver, keyed by composition position; see the remember chunk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "override onSaveInstanceState". Senior explains the id-keyed SparseArray, duplicate-id collisions, size limits and when state belongs in a ViewModel instead.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reusable quantity-stepper placed three times via <include> with the same id showed the last stepper's value in all three after rotation.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how a touch event travels through the View hierarchy: dispatchTouchEvent, onInterceptTouchEvent, onTouchEvent.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Gesture conflicts are the most common non-trivial UI bug, and the model is simple if you know it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The event enters at the Activity (Activity.dispatchTouchEvent), then the window's DecorView, then goes down: each ViewGroup's dispatchTouchEvent first asks its own onInterceptTouchEvent; if false the event goes to the child under the pointer, if no child handles it (or it intercepts) the ViewGroup's own onTouchEvent runs. If a view returns true from onTouchEvent, it becomes the target for the rest of the gesture. If nobody consumes, it bubbles back up.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity.dispatchTouchEvent
  -> DecorView -> ViewGroup.dispatchTouchEvent
        ACTION_DOWN: reset state; onInterceptTouchEvent? --yes--> this.onTouchEvent
                                      | no
                                      v
                         find child under pointer (reverse draw order), child.dispatchTouchEvent
                         child true -> child becomes touch target (mFirstTouchTarget)
        later MOVE/UP: go straight to the target (intercept still asked for each event!)
        parent intercepts later -> child gets ACTION_CANCEL, parent takes over

Key rules: a view that returns false for ACTION_DOWN never sees the rest of that gesture. onInterceptTouchEvent is not called for DOWN if FLAG_DISALLOW_INTERCEPT was set by a child via requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true), and is called per event otherwise while a target exists. OnTouchListener runs before onTouchEvent; if it returns true onTouchEvent (and therefore performClick via onTouchEvent) is skipped. onClick fires in onTouchEvent on ACTION_UP when the view is clickable and was pressed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SwipeLayout(ctx: Context, a: AttributeSet?) : FrameLayout(ctx, a) {
    private val slop = ViewConfiguration.get(ctx).scaledTouchSlop
    private var downX = 0f
    override fun onInterceptTouchEvent(e: MotionEvent): Boolean {
        when (e.actionMasked) {
            MotionEvent.ACTION_DOWN -> downX = e.x
            MotionEvent.ACTION_MOVE -> if (abs(e.x - downX) > slop) return true
        }
        return false
    }
    override fun onTouchEvent(e: MotionEvent): Boolean = true // consume once we own the gesture
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Intercepting on DOWN, which makes children unclickable.
  • Returning false from onTouchEvent on DOWN while expecting later MOVE events.
  • Not handling ACTION_CANCEL (leaves pressed/drag state stuck).
  • Ignoring touch slop and multi-pointer indices.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the child see when a parent intercepts mid-gesture? → One ACTION_CANCEL, then nothing.
  2. Where does performClick fit and why does lint warn about it? → For accessibility, custom onTouchEvent must call performClick() on UP so click listeners and accessibility services fire.
  3. Difference between onTouch and onTouchEvent? → Listener vs view override; listener runs first and can swallow.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the three method names. Senior knows target tracking, DOWN-only discovery, CANCEL, disallow-intercept flag and the accessibility performClick requirement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A swipe-to-dismiss row ate taps on its inner buttons because it intercepted on DOWN.

questions.promptHtml: A horizontal swipeable view sits inside a vertical scroller. How do onInterceptTouchEvent and requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent resolve the conflict, and why does the "obvious" fix sometimes break it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the standard gesture-conflict question; the follow-ups expose real understanding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Whoever sees the gesture first and crosses the touch slop decides. The parent scroller intercepts when vertical movement exceeds slop; the child can call parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true) once it detects the gesture is horizontal, which stops ancestors intercepting until UP/CANCEL. The robust approach is to decide by dominant axis after slop, not on DOWN, and to re-allow interception on CANCEL/UP.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• On DOWN, both parent and child start tracking. Parent's onInterceptTouchEvent is polled on every MOVE. If the vertical delta crosses slop first, the parent intercepts and the child gets CANCEL.
  • The child fix is to call requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true) on MOVE when |dx| > |dy| and |dx| > slop. It sets FLAG_DISALLOW_INTERCEPT on every ancestor and is reset on DOWN, not automatically otherwise: you must call it with false on UP/CANCEL if you want a later gesture in the same dispatch to be interceptable (in practice the flag resets at the next DOWN).
  • Why the obvious fix breaks: calling disallow on DOWN means a vertical swipe starting on the child can never scroll the parent (dead zone). Calling it too late is useless because the parent already intercepted. Also, if the child is itself scrollable in the vertical direction at its limits, you should hand control back: check canScrollHorizontally(direction) before disallowing.
  • Modern replacement: make the child implement nested scrolling (NestedScrollingChild) so the protocol arbitrates, rather than hand-rolled intercept hacks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
override fun onTouchEvent(e: MotionEvent): Boolean {
    when (e.actionMasked) {
        MotionEvent.ACTION_DOWN -> { startX = e.x; startY = e.y }
        MotionEvent.ACTION_MOVE -> {
            val dx = e.x - startX; val dy = e.y - startY
            val horizontal = abs(dx) > slop && abs(dx) > abs(dy)
            parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(horizontal && canScrollHorizontally(-dx.sign.toInt()))
        }
        MotionEvent.ACTION_UP, MotionEvent.ACTION_CANCEL -> parent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(false)
    }
    return super.onTouchEvent(e)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Disallow-intercept on DOWN creates dead zones.
  • Forgetting that the parent only checks intercept while it has no target or when the flag is clear.
  • Using fixed pixel thresholds instead of scaledTouchSlop.
  • Not checking whether the child can still scroll in that direction (edge overscroll should pass to the parent).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does ViewPager2 containing a horizontal RecyclerView work? → ViewPager2 wraps its RecyclerView and itself is the nested-scroll aware parent; nested same-orientation scrollers still need explicit code.
  2. Is the flag inherited by siblings? → No, it is set on ancestors in the dispatch chain only.
  3. How does NestedScrollView do this without hacks? → Via the nested-scrolling protocol; see Q252.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "call requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent". Senior decides by dominant axis after slop, handles edge handoff and CANCEL cleanup, and prefers the nested-scrolling protocol.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A carousel inside a pull-to-refresh container sometimes triggered refresh while swiping horizontally with a slight upward drift.

questions.contextHtml: A home screen has a vertical NestedScrollView containing a promo banner ViewPager2 (horizontal) and, below it, a horizontal RecyclerView of 12 category chips. After a refactor from ScrollView to SwipeRefreshLayout > NestedScrollView, support tickets say "banner swipe sometimes triggers refresh" and "chips feel stuck, need two swipes". Crash-free is fine; ticket volume is 1.2k/week out of 400k DAU. Logcat shows nothing. QA reproduces only on a Pixel 6 and a Galaxy A14, not the emulator. A teammate added requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent(true) on ACTION_DOWN in the chips RecyclerView as a quick fix; tickets for "can't scroll the page when finger starts on chips" appear next day.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose it, fix it properly and explain why the quick fix regressed.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disallow intercept on the child." That is the exact quick fix that caused the regression, and it ignores slop and device differences.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which versions of ViewPager2/RecyclerView/SwipeRefreshLayout? Did the scaled touch slop differ (high-density devices)? Does the chips area have padding that the finger starts in? Is the gesture diagonal? Did the same code work before wrapping with SwipeRefreshLayout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the DOWN-time disallow (it creates a dead zone for vertical scroll) via a hotfix flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SwipeRefreshLayout intercepts on small downward deltas before the horizontal view decides. (b) The horizontal child never tells ancestors the gesture is horizontal. (c) Slop differs per device density so thresholds measured in px behave differently. (d) Adding a wrapper changed intercept order.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log MotionEvent action sequences with a debug touch logger from dispatchTouchEvent at each level; use adb shell getevent or "Pointer location" in Developer options; compare ViewConfiguration.scaledTouchSlop across devices; bisect the layout change.
  5. Root cause: Pull-to-refresh claims the gesture on first downward slop movement, before the horizontal child has crossed its own slop and asked for disallow. Diagonal swipes fire refresh. The chips RecyclerView needed two swipes because the first gesture was consumed (CANCEL) by the parent.
  6. Fix: Short-term: wrap horizontal containers in a helper that calls requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent only when |dx| > |dy| and |dx| > slop, resetting on UP/CANCEL. Long-term: use nested-scroll aware widgets (ViewPager2 already coordinates with its parent; ensure SwipeRefreshLayout only wraps the vertical scroller), and test with a gesture-injection test.
  7. Prevention: Instrumented tests that inject diagonal swipes via UiAutomator/MotionEvent sequences; touch-conflict checklist in review; limit nesting of same-axis scrollers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set disallow on DOWN globally, and not raise the slop to a magic constant. I would not rewrite the screen in Compose just for this (though Compose's nested-scroll model is a legit long-term reason).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the banner autoscrolls? → Pause on touch DOWN and resume on UP/CANCEL; autoscroll posts setCurrentItem and must not fight the gesture.
  • Why only two devices? → Different slop/density and OEM touch sampling; ratio of diagonal drift matters.
  • Does android:nestedScrollingEnabled help? → For RecyclerView inside NestedScrollView it enables nested scroll participation; it does not arbitrate horizontal vs vertical.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shopping app's "swipe the carousel" refreshed the page for 3% of sessions; the cause was a refresh layout intercepting at 8 px while the carousel waited for 21 px slop.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests disallow-on-DOWN.
  • Hire: Explains axis-based disallow and CANCEL.
  • Strong hire: Adds device-specific slop, touch logging, test automation and nested scroll protocol use.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the nested scrolling protocol (NestedScrollingChild/Parent, versions 2 and 3). How is it different from touch interception, and where does it show up in the framework?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the modern, correct way to coordinate scrollers (CoordinatorLayout, collapsing toolbars, pull to refresh). Few candidates know it beyond the name.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Instead of a parent stealing the touch stream, the scrolling child reports each scroll delta to its parent first (dispatchNestedPreScroll), the parent consumes what it wants, the child scrolls with the remainder, then reports what it consumed and what is left over (dispatchNestedScroll). The same exists for flings. The child keeps the touch gesture, but the parent can still collapse headers or scroll its own content. NestedScrollingChild2 added input types touch vs non-touch (fling), and Child3 added a consumed output for the unconsumed distance, available since androidx.core 1.1.0.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
child ACTION_DOWN: startNestedScroll(axes, type)  -> finds nested-scrolling-enabled parent chain
child ACTION_MOVE: dy
   dispatchNestedPreScroll(dx, dy, consumed[], offsetInWindow, type)  -> parent eats part (collapse toolbar)
   child scrolls its content by (dy - consumed)
   dispatchNestedScroll(consumedX, consumedY, unconsumedX, unconsumedY, offset, type, consumed[]) -> parent gets leftover (overscroll, pull-to-refresh)
child fling:  dispatchNestedPreFling -> parent may take it; else child flings; dispatchNestedFling
child UP:     stopNestedScroll(type)
  • Parent side: onStartNestedScroll, onNestedPreScroll, onNestedScroll, onStopNestedScroll.
  • RecyclerView and NestedScrollView are children and (NestedScrollView) parents. CoordinatorLayout + AppBarLayout.ScrollingViewBehavior is the classic implementation; SwipeRefreshLayout is a parent.
  • Non-touch type (Child2/3) matters because a fling continues after the finger left; the parent needs to know whether the scroll is driven by touch or by fling to avoid fighting.
  • Compare to Compose NestedScrollConnection (pre-scroll/post-scroll/pre-fling/post-fling): same model, different API (see the Compose modifiers chunk).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CollapsingParent(ctx: Context) : FrameLayout(ctx), NestedScrollingParent3 {
    private val helper = NestedScrollingParentHelper(this)
    override fun onStartNestedScroll(child: View, target: View, axes: Int, type: Int) =
        axes and ViewCompat.SCROLL_AXIS_VERTICAL != 0
    override fun onNestedScrollAccepted(child: View, target: View, axes: Int, type: Int) =
        helper.onNestedScrollAccepted(child, target, axes, type)
    override fun onNestedPreScroll(target: View, dx: Int, dy: Int, consumed: IntArray, type: Int) {
        val eat = if (dy > 0) min(dy, headerVisibleHeight()) else 0
        if (eat > 0) { collapseBy(eat); consumed[1] = eat }
    }
    override fun onNestedScroll(t: View, dxC: Int, dyC: Int, dxU: Int, dyU: Int, type: Int, consumed: IntArray) { /* overscroll */ }
    override fun onNestedScroll(t: View, dxC: Int, dyC: Int, dxU: Int, dyU: Int, type: Int) {}
    override fun onStopNestedScroll(target: View, type: Int) = helper.onStopNestedScroll(target, type)
    private fun headerVisibleHeight() = 0
    private fun collapseBy(px: Int) {}
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Nested scrollers in the same direction with wrap_content heights: the inner list measures all items (see lists chunk).
  • Forgetting ViewCompat.setNestedScrollingEnabled / isNestedScrollingEnabled on API < 21 views.
  • Mishandling the type parameter, so fling and drag double-consume.
  • Expecting it to solve a horizontal-in-vertical conflict: it coordinates same-axis motion; cross-axis still needs intercept logic or the widget's built-in handling.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who initiates? → The child, on DOWN via startNestedScroll.
  2. What does consumed[] mean? → An out-array where the parent writes how many px it used so the child scrolls the remainder.
  3. Why was Child3 needed? → To report unconsumed distance back to the child (e.g. overscroll/stretch effects) in a consistent protocol; verify exact semantic in the reference when asked.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "CoordinatorLayout handles it". Senior explains pre/post phases, the touch/non-touch type split and how it replaced intercept hacks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A collapsing header jittered during fling because custom code consumed in onNestedScroll instead of onNestedPreScroll.

questions.promptHtml: When would you choose ConstraintLayout over nested LinearLayouts (or FrameLayout/RelativeLayout), and when is ConstraintLayout the wrong choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgment and measurement rather than dogma.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ConstraintLayout gives a flat hierarchy for complex relative arrangements, which avoids deep nesting and the double-measure cost of weighted LinearLayouts. For a simple row or column, a single LinearLayout/FrameLayout is cheaper and clearer. I choose based on depth and measure cost shown in Layout Inspector or a trace, not by default.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The official guidance: nested LinearLayouts can create deep hierarchies and nested layout_weight means each child is measured twice; flattening with ConstraintLayout as root yields a two-level hierarchy (per the Android layout-optimisation guide). ConstraintLayout solves linear constraints (Cassowary-derived solver), measures children typically once for wrap/fixed dimensions, but match_constraint (0dp) children with chains, barriers or percentage dimensions can trigger a second measure pass. It has its own overhead (solver setup, constraint graph) so for 3 stacked TextViews a LinearLayout wins.

Need Choice
Simple stack, no weights LinearLayout
Overlap/single child FrameLayout
Complex relations, responsive, chains, barriers ConstraintLayout
Equal-width cells in a grid GridLayout/RecyclerView grid/ConstraintLayout guideline
Animations between states ConstraintLayout + MotionLayout (extra cost)

Practical points: Barrier and Group are helpful; Guidelines avoid wrapper views; large chains with weights are not free; the XML is more verbose; tooling is excellent. In RecyclerView item layouts, flat is the target because inflation + measure repeat per item. Version numbers of ConstraintLayout (2.x) change solver details, verify against the release you ship.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
    android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="wrap_content">
    <ImageView android:id="@+id/avatar" android:layout_width="48dp" android:layout_height="48dp"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent" app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"/>
    <TextView android:id="@+id/title" android:layout_width="0dp" android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toEndOf="@id/avatar" app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="@id/avatar"/>
</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating ConstraintLayout as automatically faster.
  • Wrapping a ConstraintLayout in another ConstraintLayout.
  • Using match_parent inside ConstraintLayout (deprecated behaviour; use 0dp).
  • Heavy use of chains with weights and percent in list items without measuring.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you measure the difference? → Perfetto measure/layout slice durations, Layout Inspector, Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric on a scrolling list.
  2. What is a Barrier vs Guideline? → Barrier moves with views' extents; Guideline is a fixed/percent line.
  3. Does Compose have this problem? → Compose measures each child once by contract (single-pass), so nested Rows/Columns do not blow up; see the layout chunk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "ConstraintLayout is flatter, so faster". Senior states when it is slower, cites the weight double-pass and validates with traces.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed card moved from two nested weighted LinearLayouts to ConstraintLayout and saved ~1.5 ms measure per item on a low-end device.

questions.promptHtml: What do <include>, <merge> and ViewStub each do, and what are their limitations?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical layout-optimisation tools; common in code review.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: <include> reuses a layout file at inflate time. <merge> removes a redundant root by letting the included children attach straight to the parent. ViewStub is a zero-size invisible placeholder that inflates its layout only when you call inflate() or make it visible, then replaces itself, which defers inflation cost for rarely shown UI like error states.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• include inflates the referenced layout into the parent; overriding android:id or layout params on the <include> tag overrides the included root's. If you override layout_* attributes you must set both layout_width and layout_height.
  • merge as root: it has no view of its own; the layout must be inflated with a parent and attachToRoot=true (or be <include>d), otherwise inflate throws InflateException: <merge /> can be used only with a valid ViewGroup root and attachToRoot=true. Lint flags FrameLayout roots without background/padding as merge candidates.
  • ViewStub costs almost nothing before inflation (it does not draw, measure to 0, and holds only a few fields). inflate() returns the inflated view; the stub removes itself from the parent. After inflation findViewById(stubId) returns null; the inflated root takes the inflatedId. It cannot be re-stubbed; to hide again use visibility on the inflated view. It cannot be used inside <merge> roots (ViewStub needs a parent to insert into; verify the case before relying on it).
  • With view binding, include yields nested binding properties only if the included tag has an id; ViewStub exposes ViewStubProxy-like access only with data binding, with view binding you get the ViewStub and call inflate().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val stub = binding.errorStub                 // ViewStub from binding
val errorRoot = if (state.isError) stub.inflate() else null
// or: stub.visibility = View.VISIBLE (inflates once)
<ViewStub android:id="@+id/errorStub" android:layout="@layout/view_error"
    android:inflatedId="@+id/errorRoot" android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="wrap_content"/>

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling inflate() twice: IllegalStateException: ViewStub must have a valid parent / "already inflated".
  • Using merge with attachToRoot=false.
  • Expecting the stub id to remain after inflation.
  • Overusing ViewStub for always-visible content (adds complexity, no gain).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does ViewStub save memory or time? → Both at start: skips inflating that subtree and its views until needed; once inflated costs are the same.
  2. Does include add a ViewGroup level? → Only the root of the included layout; use merge to avoid it.
  3. Alternative for heavy screens? → Async inflation, fragment/lazy sections, or Compose if branches that compose only when shown.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines them. Senior knows the merge attachToRoot rule, the stub self-removal and when the saving is real.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen inflated 4 rarely used banners at startup; moving them to ViewStubs trimmed ~12 ms from first layout on a low-end device.

questions.contextHtml: A legacy product-detail Activity takes 520 ms from onCreate to first frame on a low-end device (2 GB RAM, Android 11), with setContentView accounting for 310 ms in a method trace. The layout XML is 380 lines, 140 views, max depth 14, with three nested weight LinearLayouts, 20 <include>s and several rarely used sections (reviews, Q&A, warranty). Startup p90 for this screen is a product KPI (target < 300 ms). Release build, R8 on. A teammate suggests "just convert to Compose in one sprint".
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut inflation and first-layout cost without a rewrite, and how do you prove it worked?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use ViewBinding" (binding does not change inflation cost) or "move it to a background thread" without knowing the constraints on view creation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 310 ms cold or warm (first inflation loads resources and classes)? How much is XML parse vs view construction vs measure/layout? Are there custom views with heavy constructors? Can sections be deferred below the fold? What is the minSdk?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Defer below-the-fold sections with ViewStub and show a skeleton for first paint.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Many views and heavy ones (e.g. WebView, MaterialCardView shadows, big drawables) constructed up front. (b) Deep hierarchy with weights makes first measure expensive (see Q246). (c) Drawable/resource loading on the main thread (vector inflation). (d) LayoutInflater reflection/constructor lookup cost for custom views, mostly first time per class.
  4. How I'd verify each: System trace (inflate slices, Choreographer#doFrame after), method sampling in Android Studio profiler, Layout Inspector for depth/counts, Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric/FrameTimingMetric, Trace.beginSection around setContentView phases.
  5. Root cause: Inflation cost scales with the number of views and attributes parsed and with first-use class loading; layout cost scales with depth and double-measure parents. Both are paid on the main thread before first frame.
  6. Fix: Short-term: ViewStub for the three sections; flatten the top part with ConstraintLayout; merge for includes; delete invisible/redundant parents flagged by lint. Medium-term: AsyncLayoutInflater (androidx.asynclayoutinflater) for the heavy subtrees (note it does not support <merge> and views must not rely on a Looper at construction, and it cannot use inflaters with a custom Factory2 that touches the UI), or pre-inflate in a prior screen's idle time. Long-term: Compose for new sections via ComposeView (see interop chunk).
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark guard in CI with a regression threshold; lint UselessParent, NestedWeights, depth limit (default 10 per the layout optimisation guide); view-count budget in review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cache a full inflated tree across Activity instances (context/leak risks) and I would not do big-bang Compose before measuring what dominates; async inflation adds race conditions around state restore.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the cost is in the first-ever LayoutInflater call in the process? → Baseline Profiles cover class loading/JIT of the inflation path; see A6 startup.
  • Can ViewBinding be async? → You can run Binding.inflate inside AsyncLayoutInflater's result via bind(view); the inflate itself still follows the same limits.
  • Why not setContentView on a worker thread? → Views must be created with the correct Context and touched on the UI thread afterwards; AsyncLayoutInflater handles the safe pattern.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A catalogue screen dropped from 480 ms to 290 ms by deferring three sections and removing four redundant parents; the Macrobenchmark guard later caught a PR that added a 40-view promo block.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests rewriting or moving inflate to a thread blindly.
  • Hire: Names ViewStub, flattening and lint, and measures.
  • Strong hire: Separates parse/construct/measure costs, uses async inflation correctly and adds CI guards.

questions.promptHtml: Explain hardware-accelerated rendering for Views, the three layer types, and when setLayerType helps or hurts.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Layer misuse is a classic cause of memory spikes and invisible-view bugs; senior engineers must reason about GPU memory and invalidation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With hardware acceleration, views record drawing commands into display lists that the RenderThread replays on the GPU; only invalidated views re-record. LAYER_TYPE_NONE is the default; HARDWARE caches a view as a GPU texture so animating alpha/translation/scale/rotation doesn't redraw its content; SOFTWARE renders to a bitmap and is also the escape hatch for unsupported Canvas operations. Hardware layers cost video memory and a re-render when content changes, so enable them only during an animation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the official docs: hardware acceleration is on by default if target API >= 14 and can be controlled at application, activity, window and view levels; you can disable per view with a software layer but cannot enable per view or disable at window level. Display list model: invalidate hierarchy -> record dirty display lists -> draw display lists. Setting alpha on a ListView only changes the parent's display list (SaveLayerAlpha, Restore) and does not re-run child drawing.

Layer trade-offs:

  • HARDWARE layer: efficient transform/alpha animation, but memory = width x height x 4 bytes (a full-screen 1080x2400 RGBA layer is about 10.4 MB) and any invalidate() re-renders the layer texture, so animating content plus a layer can be slower than none.
  • SOFTWARE layer: bitmap-backed software render, then uploaded; slow for large areas, needed for unsupported ops (the docs list setMaskFilter, setLinearText as unsupported, many others supported only from certain API levels).
  • View.setAlpha on a view with overlapping children triggers an offscreen buffer (doubling fill-rate cost per the docs); hasOverlappingRendering() = false allows alpha without a layer when children don't overlap.
  • Modern guidance: view properties animate through RenderNode properties; Compose graphicsLayer is the equivalent concept.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun View.flip(duration: Long = 300) {
    setLayerType(View.LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE, null)
    animate().rotationY(180f).setDuration(duration)
        .withEndAction { setLayerType(View.LAYER_TYPE_NONE, null) }   // free the texture
        .start()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving hardware layers on permanently (VRAM waste, stale content).
  • Using a software layer on a large scrolling container (CPU draw each frame).
  • Putting a hardware layer on a view whose content changes every frame.
  • Assuming a Canvas call works on every API level (e.g. clipPath on API < 18).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does ViewPropertyAnimator.alpha auto-use a layer? → ViewPropertyAnimator can use withLayer() to wrap the animation in a hardware layer for its duration.
  2. What does a layer do to overdraw tools? → Layers show as an extra composited surface; GPU overdraw coloring reflects blending, not memory.
  3. How do you check acceleration at draw time? → canvas.isHardwareAccelerated (preferred over view.isHardwareAccelerated per the docs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "hardware layer makes animations faster". Senior quantifies memory, ties it to invalidation, and scopes the layer to the animation lifetime.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A permanent hardware layer on a full-screen parallax container added ~10 MB GPU memory per instance; four overlapping instances caused OOM-style GPU texture eviction on low-end devices.

questions.contextHtml: A news feed screen shows 55% of pixels in red/pink in "Debug GPU overdraw". Frame timing on a low-end device (GPU-bound, 60 Hz) shows 18 ms p90 GPU work during scroll, with jank 14%. The window background is the theme default white, the root LinearLayout has android:background="#FFF", the RecyclerView also has a white background, each card has a white CardView with a white inner ConstraintLayout background, and a decorative gradient ImageView is stacked under the text. Crashes: none. Team says "Compose will fix it".
questions.promptHtml: How do you find and remove overdraw, what is the target, and what won't help?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove backgrounds until it's blue" without understanding hidden-by-opaque rules or measuring GPU time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is jank GPU-bound or CPU-bound (verify with the frame timeline)? Are cards opaque by design? Are there translucent decorations/shadows/elevation on every item? Any alpha animations?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the root and RecyclerView backgrounds that are fully covered, and set the theme windowBackground to the real base colour (or null where the root covers it).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Stacked opaque backgrounds (window + root + list + card + inner). (b) A full-bleed decorative view under text. (c) Many shadows/elevation (CardView shadow blur is costly). (d) Translucent overlays or alpha creating offscreen buffers.
  4. How I'd verify each: Developer options -> Debug GPU overdraw (colours: no colour = 0x, blue 1x, green 2x, pink 3x, red 4x+; verify per OS version), Perfetto GPU/RenderThread slices and frame timeline, dumpsys gfxinfo per-frame stats, Profile GPU rendering bars, Layout Inspector 3D view.
  5. Root cause: Each opaque layer repaints every pixel beneath it. The official rule of thumb is to avoid drawing more than about 2.5x the pixel count of the screen per frame (transparent pixels count). Fill-rate dominates on low-end GPUs.
  6. Fix: Remove redundant backgrounds, android:windowBackground only where needed, flatten card layout so one view paints the card, replace gradient ImageView with a drawable background on the card or clipToOutline shape, avoid per-item alpha, reduce elevation on list items, hasOverlappingRendering=false where safe, and use canvas.clipRect in custom views to skip hidden regions.
  7. Prevention: Overdraw screenshot checks in design review, a Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric guard on low-end, lint rules for redundant backgrounds ("Overdraw: Painting regions more than once").
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't remove the window background on activities with transparent areas (flash on start) and wouldn't chase blue everywhere; some overdraw (shadows, text on cards) is intended.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does Compose avoid overdraw? → No: stacked Modifier.background also overdraws; the tooling is the same.
  • What about CardView on Android 12+? → Elevation shadows are rendered by the platform; many shadowed items remain a GPU cost; use flatter cards if profiling shows it.
  • How do I distinguish overdraw from texture upload jank? → Perfetto shows GPU completion time vs UploadTexture/bitmap decode slices.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Removing five redundant white backgrounds dropped jank from 14% to 6% on the budget device class, with no visual change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cites the colour tool only.
  • Hire: Removes layers, explains the 2.5x rule, verifies with GPU metrics.
  • Strong hire: Distinguishes GPU vs CPU jank, handles window background trade-offs, adds regression guard.

questions.promptHtml: Why must a Fragment null out its view binding in onDestroyView? What exactly leaks otherwise, and how does View Binding differ from findViewById and Data Binding?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Binding leaks are the most common memory leak in Fragment-based apps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Fragment instance outlives its view hierarchy (e.g. on the back stack, onDestroyView is called but the Fragment object remains). If the Fragment keeps a reference to the binding, the whole old view tree, with its Context/Activity reference, bitmaps and adapters, stays reachable until the Fragment itself is destroyed. So the binding must be cleared in onDestroyView. View binding is generated, type-safe and null-safe direct fields with no runtime lookup; data binding adds layout expressions/two-way binding at the cost of annotation processing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fragment (long life) --_binding--> Binding --> root View --> children --> Activity context, adapters, listeners
onDestroyView: view gone from window but still referenced => retained

Per the official docs: "Fragments outlive their views", so clean up the binding reference in onDestroyView. Other holdouts: adapters assigned to RecyclerView (recyclerView.adapter = null is needed if the adapter is a Fragment field and holds view references), ViewPager2 callbacks, viewLifecycleOwner observers (use viewLifecycleOwner, not this, so observers die with the view), FragmentContainerView/DialogFragment listeners, and ValueAnimator listeners.

View Binding facts from the docs: compile-time generated classes, no annotation processing (faster builds than data binding), no layout variables/expressions, tools:viewBindingIgnore to skip a layout, bind() for already inflated views, @Nullable fields for views not in all layout configurations, and tools:viewBindingType to unify types across configuration variants.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_profile) {
    private var _binding: FragmentProfileBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentProfileBinding.bind(view)
        viewModel.state.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { binding.name.text = it.name }
    }
    override fun onDestroyView() {
        binding.list.adapter = null   // break adapter -> view references
        _binding = null
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keeping lateinit var binding and never clearing it.
  • Observing LiveData/Flow with this rather than viewLifecycleOwner.
  • Accessing binding after onDestroyView from a callback: NPE (_binding!!).
  • Assuming Activities have the same problem: an Activity's view dies with it, so no.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you auto-clear it? → A ViewBindingDelegate observing viewLifecycleOwner or Fragment.viewLifecycleOwnerLiveData to null on destroy.
  2. Does findViewById also leak? → Same: any field holding a View beyond onDestroyView.
  3. How do you catch it? → LeakCanary reports Fragment.mView leaks ("Fragment received Fragment#onDestroyView() callback but view is still reachable"; verify wording in your version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the _binding = null pattern. Senior explains the lifetime mismatch, the other retention paths and uses viewLifecycleOwner and LeakCanary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tabbed screen retained 6 old fragment view trees (about 18 MB) via cached bindings, which showed up as OOM on 2 GB devices after 20 tab switches.

questions.contextHtml:
LeakCanary on QA builds reports: Fragment.mView still referenced after onDestroyView for OrdersFragment, retaining 4.2 MB. Production: OOM crash rate for this flow is 0.6% (about 2,400 sessions/day of 400k) on devices with <= 3 GB RAM, after users navigate list -> detail -> back repeatedly. Code:

class OrdersFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_orders) {
    private lateinit var binding: FragmentOrdersBinding
    private val adapter = OrdersAdapter { id -> viewModel.open(id) }
    private val refreshHandler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
        binding = FragmentOrdersBinding.bind(view)
        binding.list.adapter = adapter
        viewModel.orders.observe(this) { adapter.submitList(it) }
        refreshHandler.postDelayed({ binding.swipe.isRefreshing = false }, 5000)
    }
}

Red herring: the adapter's image loading uses a bitmap pool, which looks heavy but is bounded.
questions.promptHtml: Find every retention path and fix them. Why does it only OOM after repeated navigation?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set binding = null in onDestroyView." Misses the observer on this, the adapter-to-RecyclerView link and the delayed handler.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the Fragment on the back stack when navigating to detail (so onDestroyView runs but the Fragment lives)? Navigation library? Is the adapter holding ViewHolders or a RecyclerView reference?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Clear binding and the adapter reference in onDestroyView, remove the handler callbacks, ship as a patch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lateinit var binding retains the view tree for the Fragment's life. (b) observe(this) keeps a lambda that captures adapter/binding until the Fragment dies, and re-adds a new observer each time the view is recreated (duplicate observers). (c) adapter is a Fragment field attached to the RecyclerView; RecyclerView's mAdapter and the adapter's observers chain to views. (d) The delayed postDelayed runnable captures binding and the Fragment for 5 s.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary leak trace reference path (OrdersFragment.binding -> ... -> mView); Android Studio heap dump, filter for OrdersFragment/FragmentOrdersBinding instance counts after 10 navigations; a test that navigates N times and asserts instance count.
  5. Root cause: Fragment lifetime (back stack) exceeds view lifetime; every view-lifetime object is stored in a Fragment-lifetime field. Each navigation recreates a view tree while the old ones remain referenced (multiple observers each hold the previous binding), hence the staircase growth until OOM.
  6. Fix:
class OrdersFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_orders) {
    private var _binding: FragmentOrdersBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!
    private var adapter: OrdersAdapter? = null
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
    private val stopRefresh = Runnable { _binding?.swipe?.isRefreshing = false }

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, s: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentOrdersBinding.bind(view)
        val a = OrdersAdapter { id -> viewModel.open(id) }.also { adapter = it }
        binding.list.adapter = a
        viewModel.orders.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { a.submitList(it) }
        handler.postDelayed(stopRefresh, 5000)
    }
    override fun onDestroyView() {
        handler.removeCallbacks(stopRefresh)
        binding.list.adapter = null
        adapter = null
        _binding = null
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}
  1. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug, a lint/detekt rule banning lateinit var binding in Fragments, instance-count tests, code review checklist on view-lifetime vs fragment-lifetime.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't retainInstance or hold bitmaps statically; and I wouldn't suppress LeakCanary. Moving the 5 s refresh timer into the ViewModel/coroutine tied to viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope is cleaner than a Handler.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the adapter must survive config changes? → Keep data in the ViewModel and rebuild the adapter per view.
  • Does viewLifecycleOwner change on rotation? → A new one per view creation, which is exactly why observers must use it.
  • Would Compose have this? → Less so: composition is disposed with the view (ViewCompositionStrategy), but ComposeView in Fragments has its own leaks (see interop chunk).

sections.html: A staircase heap graph (+4 MB per navigation) was traced to observe(this) plus a cached binding; fixing both flattened the heap and dropped OOMs 90%.

  • Hire: Finds observer, adapter and handler paths, uses viewLifecycleOwner.
  • Strong hire: Explains the lifetime mismatch, verifies with heap dump counts and adds prevention tooling.

questions.promptHtml: How do you write a custom ViewGroup (say a FlowLayout)? Cover LayoutParams, onMeasure, onLayout, and the pitfalls that cause double measurement or crashes.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Custom ViewGroups combine the measure contract, LayoutParams generation and layout correctness; they reveal depth.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Override onMeasure to measure each child with measureChildWithMargins (or getChildMeasureSpec) using the parent spec minus used space, accumulate row widths/heights, and call setMeasuredDimension with resolveSizeAndState. In onLayout position every child with child.layout(l, t, r, b) using the measured sizes. Override generateLayoutParams/checkLayoutParams/generateDefaultLayoutParams so XML attributes like margins parse into your LayoutParams type. Avoid measuring a child twice per pass unless needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• onMeasure runs top-down: for each visible child (skip GONE), build its spec from your constraints and call measureChildWithMargins. For wrap-heavy layouts you measure children with AT_MOST of the remaining width, wrap to a new row when rowWidth + childWidth > maxWidth.
  • If the parent's spec is UNSPECIFIED, treat max width as unbounded.
  • onLayout(changed, l, t, r, b) uses child.measuredWidth/Height and margins. Never call measure in onLayout.
  • RTL: honour layoutDirection (use isLayoutRtl and ViewGroupCompat/LayoutDirection checks) or mirror x positions.
  • Measure twice only when forced (e.g. child heights depend on the final width); prefer a single pass. Nested double-measure compounds exponentially (see Q246).
  • Save state, clipChildren, setWillNotDraw(true) (ViewGroups don't draw by default, set setWillNotDraw(false) only if you override onDraw), and dispatchDraw for decorations.
  • LayoutParams: subclass MarginLayoutParams and override the three generate/check methods; without them addView(child) with the default params may throw ClassCastException when onMeasure casts child.layoutParams as MyParams.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FlowLayout @JvmOverloads constructor(c: Context, a: AttributeSet? = null) : ViewGroup(c, a) {
    override fun onMeasure(wSpec: Int, hSpec: Int) {
        val maxW = MeasureSpec.getSize(wSpec) - paddingLeft - paddingRight
        val unbounded = MeasureSpec.getMode(wSpec) == MeasureSpec.UNSPECIFIED
        var x = 0; var y = 0; var rowH = 0; var usedW = 0
        for (i in 0 until childCount) {
            val v = getChildAt(i); if (v.visibility == GONE) continue
            measureChildWithMargins(v, wSpec, 0, hSpec, 0)
            val lp = v.layoutParams as MarginLayoutParams
            val w = v.measuredWidth + lp.leftMargin + lp.rightMargin
            val h = v.measuredHeight + lp.topMargin + lp.bottomMargin
            if (!unbounded && x + w > maxW && x > 0) { y += rowH; x = 0; rowH = 0 }
            x += w; rowH = maxOf(rowH, h); usedW = maxOf(usedW, x)
        }
        val totalH = y + rowH + paddingTop + paddingBottom
        setMeasuredDimension(resolveSize(usedW + paddingLeft + paddingRight, wSpec), resolveSize(totalH, hSpec))
    }
    // onLayout repeats the same wrapping logic using measuredWidth/Height
    override fun onLayout(changed: Boolean, l: Int, t: Int, r: Int, b: Int) { /* position children */ }
    override fun generateLayoutParams(a: AttributeSet) = MarginLayoutParams(context, a)
    override fun generateDefaultLayoutParams() = MarginLayoutParams(WRAP_CONTENT, WRAP_CONTENT)
    override fun generateLayoutParams(p: LayoutParams) = MarginLayoutParams(p)
    override fun checkLayoutParams(p: LayoutParams) = p is MarginLayoutParams
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using measureChild and ignoring margins.
  • Computing row breaks differently in onMeasure and onLayout, which clips children.
  • Not skipping GONE children.
  • Forgetting checkLayoutParams, causing ClassCastException.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where do you cache row geometry? → Store row breaks during onMeasure and reuse in onLayout to avoid recomputation.
  2. When is a custom ViewGroup better than ConstraintLayout Flow helper? → Special packing logic or performance in a hot list; otherwise use Flow helper or Material ChipGroup/Compose FlowRow.
  3. Why can onMeasure be called with the same spec repeatedly? → Parent re-measure passes and weights; cache by isLayoutRequested if expensive.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can write onLayout. Senior handles LayoutParams, UNSPECIFIED, RTL, GONE, and measurement cost.
