questions.contextHtml: A bottom sheet with a complex map-preview card (about 60 child views, dynamic content updating every 250 ms from live data) animates in with translationY. On a low-end device the animation drops to ~35 fps; on flagship devices it's smooth. A developer added setLayerType(LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE, null) on the sheet "to make animations smooth", and left it on. Results: slide-in is now smooth, but live content updates stutter, GPU memory rose by about 9 MB (1080 x 2220 sheet), and a QA build shows a blank white flash at the end of some transitions on one OEM.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what the hardware layer did, why it helped and hurt, and what you would ship.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Hardware layers are always faster; the white flash is an OEM bug."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does content change during the slide-in? Is the sheet full-screen sized? Which OEM/GPU? Is the white flash tied to layer teardown at animation end? Android version?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Limit the layer to the animation window and pause the 250 ms updates while it runs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) During animation the layer lets the GPU transform a cached texture instead of redrawing 60 views each frame, explaining the smoothness. (b) With the layer left on, each content update invalidates the layer and re-renders the whole texture (60-view subtree) every 250 ms, plus the texture upload/composite. (c) Memory: width x height x 4 bytes = 1080 x 2220 x 4 = about 9.6 MB, matching the observed increase. (d) The flash is a layer-teardown/first-draw timing issue on a driver, or content invalidated before the layer is rebuilt.
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto frame timeline and RenderThread slices before/after; dumpsys gfxinfo GPU memory/texture stats; GPU profiler bars; toggling the layer at the end of the animation with and without delay; repro on that OEM with screen recording frame-stepping.
  5. Root cause: Layers trade redraw for texture composition. They are great for static content under transforms and bad for dynamic content because each invalidation re-renders into the texture.
  6. Fix: Enable LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE only in onAnimationStart, drop to LAYER_TYPE_NONE in onAnimationEnd (as in the official guidance), delay content updates until after the animation, and use ViewPropertyAnimator.withLayer(). If still janky on low-end, simplify the card (flatten, reduce shadows, avoid alpha on overlapping children).
  7. Prevention: A Macrobenchmark jank test on a low-end device for the sheet open; code review rule: any setLayerType must be paired with a reset.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't leave a full-screen layer on permanently, nor use LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE (CPU render + upload every change). I wouldn't blame the OEM before ruling out our end-of-animation invalidation.
sheet.animate().translationY(0f).setDuration(250).withLayer().start()

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if updates must continue during the animation? → Update a small child (not the whole subtree) and keep the layer off, or snapshot the static part into the layer and draw the live part outside it.
  • How is this in Compose? → Modifier.graphicsLayer with lambda-based properties avoids recomposition and uses RenderNode layers; same cost model.
  • Does alpha on the sheet need a layer? → Compositing alpha for overlapping children creates an offscreen buffer; a hardware layer can make it cheaper for large views (per docs).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A left-on hardware layer on a parallax header produced a steady GPU memory climb in a long session; scoping it to the animation duration removed a class of low-end OOMs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Leave it on, it works."
  • Hire: Explains texture caching vs invalidation and scopes the layer.
  • Strong hire: Computes the memory, plans benchmark verification and addresses the flash with evidence.

questions.contextHtml:
A custom AspectImageView (extends View, draws a bitmap with a fixed 16:9 ratio) is used in three places: a RecyclerView card (match_parent width, wrap_content height), a HorizontalScrollView row (wrap_content width, 120dp height), and a dialog. QA reports: card shows a 0-height image on API 29 only in one layout; in the horizontal row images are massive (full screen width); after adding 2dp padding the image is clipped. Code:

class AspectImageView(c: Context, a: AttributeSet?) : View(c, a) {
    override fun onMeasure(wSpec: Int, hSpec: Int) {
        val w = MeasureSpec.getSize(wSpec)
        val h = w * 9 / 16
        setMeasuredDimension(w, h)
    }
    override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) {
        bitmap?.let { canvas.drawBitmap(it, 0f, 0f, null) }
    }
}

Red herring: the bitmap loading library logs warnings about downsampling, unrelated.
questions.promptHtml: Explain each symptom from the code and produce a correct onMeasure.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use ConstraintLayout layout_constraintDimensionRatio instead." Valid as an alternative but doesn't explain the bugs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What specs does each parent pass (Layout Inspector shows)? Is height ever EXACTLY? Is the image allowed to letterbox? minSdk?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace with ShapeableImageView/ConstraintLayout ratio constraint (app:layout_constraintDimensionRatio="16:9") as a stop-gap if a release is imminent.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Width taken from spec size regardless of mode, so in HorizontalScrollView (UNSPECIFIED/AT_MOST with huge size) it becomes huge. (b) When the parent passes UNSPECIFIED the size can be 0 (API-dependent) so w=0, h=0: the zero-height card. (c) Height ignores an EXACTLY height spec (120dp row). (d) Padding ignored in both measure and draw.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the mode/size per spec with MeasureSpec.toString; Layout Inspector for actual sizes; unit test with View.MeasureSpec.makeMeasureSpec combos.
  5. Root cause: onMeasure assumes EXACTLY on width and ignores the height spec and padding.
  6. Fix:
override fun onMeasure(wSpec: Int, hSpec: Int) {
    val wMode = MeasureSpec.getMode(wSpec); val hMode = MeasureSpec.getMode(hSpec)
    val padH = paddingLeft + paddingRight; val padV = paddingTop + paddingBottom
    var w: Int; var h: Int
    if (wMode == MeasureSpec.EXACTLY) {
        w = MeasureSpec.getSize(wSpec)
        h = ((w - padH) * 9f / 16f).toInt() + padV
    } else if (hMode == MeasureSpec.EXACTLY) {
        h = MeasureSpec.getSize(hSpec)
        w = ((h - padV) * 16f / 9f).toInt() + padH
    } else {
        w = (bitmap?.width ?: 0) + padH               // natural size
        h = ((w - padH) * 9f / 16f).toInt() + padV
    }
    setMeasuredDimension(resolveSize(w, wSpec), resolveSize(h, hSpec))
}

and draw inside the padded area. 7. Prevention: Parameterised unit tests across all mode combinations, screenshot tests in each container, lint CustomViewStyleable/review checklist for onMeasure. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hack with post { layoutParams.height = ... } (extra layout pass, flicker). For simple ratios ConstraintLayout/ShapeableImageView plus layout_constraintDimensionRatio is less code than a custom view.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if both modes are EXACTLY and mismatch the ratio? → Respect the parent: fit/center the bitmap while drawing.
  • Why can AT_MOST height smaller than the computed size matter? → resolveSize clamps; you'd need MEASURED_STATE_TOO_SMALL via resolveSizeAndState if you want the parent to re-measure.
  • In RecyclerView does the 0-height case matter? → Yes, it can render an empty item row and break scroll offsets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hero image looked right in every test layout except inside a horizontal scroller on tablets, where it became 1200 px wide; the cause was the one-line spec read.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests different layout only.
  • Hire: Identifies mode handling and padding, produces correct code.
  • Strong hire: Adds test matrix, UNSPECIFIED subtlety, and chooses the simplest production alternative.
